ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
A large Ferris wheel at an amusement park has four seats, located \(90^\circ\) from each other and at a distance \( R \) from the axis. Each seat is attached to the wheel by a strong axle. As the Ferris wheel rotates with a constant angular velocity \( \omega \), the seats move past positions \( A \), \( B \), \( C \), and \( D \) as shown.

What force must an axle provide to keep a seat of mass \( m \) moving past position \( A \)?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The diagram shows a Ferris wheel with four seats spaced 90 degrees apart. Seat A is at the top of the wheel, B is at the right, C is at the bottom, and D is at the left. The radius from the center to the seats is labeled R, and the wheel rotates with angular velocity omega. Since A is at the top, the center of the wheel is directly below the seat at A. Reasoning: At position A, the required centripetal acceleration points downward toward the center and has magnitude R omega^2. Use downward as the positive radial direction. Gravity on the seat is downward, so it contributes +mg. Let the axle force be upward when positive; then it contributes -F_axle in the downward-positive equation. Newton's second law radially gives mg - F_axle = m R omega^2. Solving gives F_axle = mg - m R omega^2. If the radius is denoted r instead of R, this is mg - m r omega^2.

method.method_draft: Use an inertial-frame free-body diagram at the top position. First read from the image that position A is at the top of the Ferris wheel, so the wheel’s center is directly below the seat and the required centripetal acceleration is downward. From the text, use the mass m, radius R, and constant angular velocity omega. Apply radial Newton’s second law with downward toward the center as positive: gravity contributes +mg, while the axle’s supporting force at A is upward if positive, so mg - F_axle = mR omega^2. Solve for the axle force: F_axle = mg - mR omega^2, matching the standard form mg - mr omega^2 if r denotes the radius.

method.method_draft: Use the rotating-frame/effective-weight viewpoint. Read from the image that at A the seat is at the top of the wheel, so outward from the center points upward and inward points downward. From the text, take the seat to be moving in a circle of radius R with angular speed omega. In the co-rotating frame the seat is instantaneously at rest, so include a centrifugal pseudo-force of magnitude mR omega^2 upward and gravity mg downward. The axle force must make the net force zero in this rotating-frame balance: F_axle upward + mR omega^2 upward - mg downward = 0. Thus F_axle = mg - mR omega^2, equivalently mg - mr omega^2 if r is used for the radius.
